title: Core Modules & the Process
intro: Senior interviews check that you know the building blocks under every framework: EventEmitter, fs, http, process, and the ways to use more than one CPU core. A strong answer explains not only the API but what blocks the event loop, what keeps the process alive, and how it behaves during deploys and failures.

questions.title: How EventEmitter works
questions.question: How does EventEmitter work internally? When you call emit(), are the listeners run synchronously or asynchronously?
questions.short: An EventEmitter keeps a map from event name to an array of listener functions. emit() looks up that array and calls every listener synchronously, in the order they were registered, on the current call stack, then returns true if there were listeners and false if not. Nothing is queued on the event loop, so a slow listener blocks the emitter and everything after the emit call.
questions.simple: It is like a teacher reading a list of names out loud: each student on the list answers right away, one after another, and the teacher does not move on until the last one has answered.

explain.p: `EventEmitter` from `node:events` is the base class behind most of Node: streams, `http.Server`, `net.Socket`, `child_process` and `process` itself are all emitters. Internally it stores an object like `{ eventName: [listener1, listener2] }` (a single function is stored directly as an optimisation).

list: Looks up the listeners for that event name. If there are none, it returns `false` (except for `error`, see the next question).
Copies the listener array, so adding or removing listeners during an emit does not affect the current emit.
Calls each listener synchronously with the arguments you passed, with `this` set to the emitter (for normal functions, not arrow functions).
Returns `true` after the last listener has returned.

explain.caption: A typical pattern: a class extends EventEmitter and emits domain events.

explain.p: Because listeners run on the same call stack, a listener that throws will throw out of `emit()` and into the code that called it. A listener that does heavy CPU work blocks the caller. If you want a listener to do work later, the listener itself must defer it, for example with `setImmediate()` or by starting an async function.

head: Method
What it does
rows: Add a listener at the front of the list
Listener removes itself after the first call
Remove one specific listener (same function reference)
Remove all listeners, or all for one event
Returns a promise that resolves on the next event

explain.note: An async listener (`async (x) => {...}`) still starts synchronously, but emit() does not wait for its promise. If that promise rejects, the rejection is unhandled unless you enable `captureRejections`.

anim.title: emit() runs every listener right now

steps.note: We create an emitter. It starts with an empty map of event names to listener arrays.
on() appends listener A to the array for the event name order. Nothing runs yet.
Listener B is appended after A, so it will run after A.
prependListener() puts the new listener at the front of the array instead of the back.
A normal synchronous log.
emit() copies the array and calls the first listener directly on the current stack. No queue, no event loop.
Still inside emit(): listener A runs next with the argument 7.
Then listener B. Only after B returns does emit() itself return true.
Back in main. This line runs only after every listener finished, which proves emit() is synchronous.
Emitting an event with no listeners does nothing and returns false.

followups.q: How would you make listeners run asynchronously?
followups.a: Inside the listener, defer the work with `setImmediate()`, `queueMicrotask()` or by calling an async function. The emitter itself never defers.

followups.q: What is `this` inside a listener?
followups.a: For a regular function it is the emitter instance. For an arrow function it is the lexical `this`, so you cannot use `this` to reach the emitter.

followups.q: How do you await a single event?
followups.a: Use `const [value] = await events.once(emitter, "name")`. It resolves with the event arguments as an array and rejects if the emitter emits `error` first.

mistakes: Saying emit() puts listeners on the event loop or a queue. It calls them synchronously.
Assuming emit() waits for async listeners to finish. It ignores their promises.
Removing a listener with a different function reference (for example a new arrow function) and wondering why it is still there.

questions.title: 'error' event, once and leaks
questions.question: What is special about the 'error' event? And what does MaxListenersExceededWarning mean?
questions.short: If you emit 'error' and nobody listens for it, EventEmitter throws the error, which usually crashes the process. So every emitter that can fail, like a stream or socket, must have an error listener. MaxListenersExceededWarning is printed when more than 10 listeners (the default) are added for one event on one emitter; it is a hint that you are probably adding a listener per request and never removing it, which is a memory leak.
questions.simple: An unanswered 'error' is like a fire alarm with nobody in the building: Node assumes the worst and shuts everything down. The listener warning is a smoke detector telling you something keeps piling up.

explain.p: `emit('error', err)` with zero `error` listeners throws `err` (or a wrapping `ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR` if it is not an Error). Since emitters usually emit errors from inside an I/O callback, there is no surrounding try/catch, so it becomes an uncaught exception and the process exits.

explain.note: Prefer `stream.pipeline()` or `await pipeline()` from `node:stream/promises` for streams. It attaches error handling to every stream in the chain and destroys them all on failure.

list: `once(name, fn)` wraps `fn` so it removes itself before running. Good for one-off events like `ready`, `close` or `listening`.
`off(name, fn)` needs the exact same function reference you passed to `on()`. Keep it in a variable.
Even a listener added with `once()` can be removed early with `off()` using the original function; Node tracks the wrapper for you.

explain.p: Each emitter has a soft limit of 10 listeners per event name (`EventEmitter.defaultMaxListeners`). Going above it does not throw; Node prints a warning once with the event name and the count. The usual bug is attaching a listener to a long-lived object inside per-request code:

Only raise the limit with `emitter.setMaxListeners(n)` when you really expect many listeners (for example a shared `AbortSignal` used by many operations). Setting it to 0 means unlimited and hides real leaks.

explain.note: Run with `--trace-warnings` to get a stack trace showing which line added the extra listener.

anim.title: once() removes itself; 'error' throws when unhandled

steps.note: once() registers a wrapper around our function. The wrapper will remove itself the first time it runs.
First emit: the wrapper removes itself from the list, then calls our function.
Second emit: nobody is listening any more, so nothing happens and emit returns false.
The count confirms the once listener is gone.
Emitting 'error' with no error listener is special: EventEmitter throws the error itself.
Here a try/catch saves us. In real code the emit happens inside an I/O callback with no try/catch, so the process would crash.
Now we register an error listener.
With a listener present, 'error' behaves like any other event: the handler runs and nothing is thrown.

followups.q: Is MaxListenersExceededWarning an error?
followups.a: No. It is a process warning printed once per emitter and event name. The code keeps working, but it usually points to a leak.

followups.q: What is `events.errorMonitor`?
followups.a: A special symbol you can listen on to observe 'error' events (for logging or metrics) without counting as a handler. The error is still thrown if no real error listener exists.

followups.q: What does `captureRejections: true` do?
followups.a: If an async listener's promise rejects, the emitter routes the rejection to its 'error' event (or a `Symbol.for('nodejs.rejection')` method) instead of leaving an unhandled rejection.

mistakes: Forgetting error listeners on streams, sockets or child processes, causing crashes on the first network hiccup.
Silencing the warning with setMaxListeners(0) instead of fixing the leak.
Calling off() with a fresh arrow function, which never matches the registered one.

questions.title: fs: sync, callback, promises
questions.question: The fs module has sync, callback and promise versions of most functions. When would you use each, and is readFileSync ever OK?
questions.short: Sync functions block the whole event loop until the disk responds, so they must not be used in request handlers. Callback and `fs/promises` functions run the work on the libuv thread pool and let the loop keep serving others; in modern code I use `node:fs/promises` with async/await. Sync calls are fine at startup (loading config or certificates before the server listens), in CLI scripts, and in build tools where nothing else is waiting.
questions.simple: A sync read is like the only cashier leaving the till to fetch something from the back room while the queue waits. The async version sends a helper to the back room so the cashier keeps serving.

explain.h: Three flavours of the same operation
How async fs works under the hood

explain.p: Most operating systems do not offer good non-blocking file I/O, so libuv runs file operations on its thread pool (4 threads by default, set with `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` before startup). When the work is done, the result is queued back to the event loop. That means heavy file I/O, `crypto.pbkdf2`, `zlib` and `dns.lookup` all share those 4 threads.

list: At startup, before `server.listen()`: reading TLS certificates, a config file, or templates.
CLI tools and one-off scripts where only one thing is happening.
Inside `require()` itself, which is sync by design.

explain.p: Inside any request handler, message consumer or timer in a server. One `readFileSync` of a large file on a slow disk can stall every connected user for that whole time.

explain.note: For big files, use `fs.createReadStream` or `fileHandle.readableWebStream()` instead of reading everything into memory, even with the async API.
Avoid `fs.exists` before opening a file (race condition). Just open it and handle `ENOENT`.

anim.title: Sync read blocks, promise read does not

steps.note: Plain synchronous log.
readFileSync makes the main thread wait for the disk. While it waits, no timer, request or callback can run.
The file content is returned directly, so the next line runs only after the read finished.
fsp.readFile hands the work to a libuv thread pool thread and returns a pending promise immediately.
The main thread is free and keeps going while the pool thread reads the file.
The script ends. The event loop waits in the poll phase until the pool thread reports that the read finished.
The read completes. Node resolves the promise, which queues the .then callback as a microtask.
The microtask runs and prints. Nothing is left, so the process exits.

followups.q: Does increasing UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE help?
followups.a: It can, if the app is bottlenecked on file I/O, crypto or zlib running in the pool. It must be set before the pool is first used (in practice, as an env var before startup). It does not help network I/O, which does not use the pool.

followups.q: Why does fs use a thread pool but sockets do not?
followups.a: Sockets have real non-blocking OS APIs (epoll, kqueue, IOCP). Regular file I/O does not have a portable non-blocking API, so libuv fakes it with threads.

followups.q: How do you read a 5 GB file?
followups.a: Stream it with `fs.createReadStream` and process chunks, or use `readline` for line-based files. Reading it fully would exceed memory and the max string size.

mistakes: Using readFileSync or writeFileSync inside request handlers.
Thinking async fs is "truly non-blocking" at the OS level. It uses the thread pool, which can saturate.
Checking `fs.existsSync` before reading instead of handling ENOENT.

questions.title: path, __dirname, import.meta
questions.question: How do you build file paths safely in Node? Why doesn't __dirname exist in ES modules, and what do you use instead?
questions.short: I use `path.join` or `path.resolve` instead of string concatenation so separators and `..` are handled for each OS. In CommonJS, `__dirname` and `__filename` are parameters of the module wrapper function, so they simply do not exist in ES modules. In ESM I use `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename` (Node 20.11+), or on older versions `fileURLToPath(new URL('.', import.meta.url))`.
questions.simple: __dirname is like a sticker CommonJS puts on each file saying where it lives. ES modules do not get that sticker, but they can read their own address (import.meta.url) and work it out.

explain.h: Relative paths are relative to the process, not the file

explain.p: `fs.readFile('./data.json')` resolves against `process.cwd()`, the folder you started Node from. If you start the app from a different folder, it breaks. To load a file next to your module, build the path from the module's own location.

When a path comes from user input, `path.join(base, userInput)` is not safe on its own, because `../../etc/passwd` is still allowed. Resolve the full path and check it is still inside the base folder.

explain.note: `import.meta.url` is a `file://` URL, not a path. Many fs APIs accept URL objects directly: `fs.readFile(new URL("./data.json", import.meta.url))`.

followups.q: What is the difference between path.join and path.resolve?
followups.a: join just glues segments and normalises them. resolve processes from right to left until it builds an absolute path, using cwd if needed. A segment starting with / resets resolve.

followups.q: What is path.posix / path.win32?
followups.a: Explicit versions of the module for one platform. Useful when you must build URL-like or POSIX paths on Windows, for example S3 keys.

mistakes: Using relative paths with fs and assuming they are relative to the source file.
Building paths with string concatenation and "/" which breaks on Windows.
Trusting path.join to prevent directory traversal.

questions.title: The http module and streams
questions.question: Without Express, how do you build an HTTP server in Node? What kind of objects are req and res?
questions.short: `http.createServer(handler)` creates a server; the handler gets `req`, an `http.IncomingMessage` which is a Readable stream, and `res`, an `http.ServerResponse` which is a Writable stream. The body is not parsed for you: you read chunks from `req` and set headers and write to `res`, finishing with `res.end()`. Because they are streams you can pipe large bodies without buffering, and you must handle errors and always end the response.
questions.simple: The request is a pipe of water coming in and the response is a pipe going out. Node gives you the pipes, not a full bucket, so you decide whether to collect the water or pass it straight through.

explain.caption: A minimal router and JSON echo with no framework.

explain.h: What you get and what you do not

list: `req.method`, `req.url` (path + query string, not parsed), `req.headers` (lower-cased keys).
No body parsing, no routing, no query parsing: use `new URL(req.url, "http://localhost")` for the query.
`res.statusCode`, `res.setHeader`, `res.writeHead`, `res.write`, `res.end`.
Headers are sent with the first `write` or `end`. Calling `setHeader` after that throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`.
Limit body size: count bytes while reading and stop with 413 if too large.

Timeouts: `server.requestTimeout` (default 300s in Node 18+), `server.headersTimeout`, `server.keepAliveTimeout` (5s default). Behind a load balancer, keep-alive timeout should be longer than the LB idle timeout.
Always end the response, including on errors, or the client hangs until a timeout.

explain.note: Express, Fastify and Koa are all built on `http.createServer`. Their `req`/`res` are the same stream objects with extra helpers.

anim.title: A POST request flowing through the streams

steps.note: The server starts listening on port 3000. Nothing runs until a connection arrives.
A client sends a POST. Node parses the request line and headers, creates req and res, and calls our handler. The body has not been read yet.
We attach a data listener. That switches req into flowing mode, and the first chunk is delivered.
More data arrives in later event loop turns. Each chunk is appended.
The client finished sending. req emits 'end', so we know the whole body is here.
writeHead sets the status and headers. They are buffered and go out with the first body bytes.
res.end writes the JSON and finishes the response. Forgetting end() would leave the client waiting.

followups.q: Why might you see ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT?
followups.a: Something tried to set a header or status after the response already started sending, often a handler that calls res.end and then also calls next(err) or sends again.

followups.q: What happens if the client disconnects mid-response?
followups.a: The response emits 'close' before 'finish' and writes fail. Use pipeline or listen for 'close' so you can stop work like DB queries or file reads.

followups.q: What is keep-alive?
followups.a: HTTP/1.1 reuses the same TCP connection for many requests. Node keeps idle connections open for `keepAliveTimeout` (5s by default) before closing them.

mistakes: Expecting req.body to exist without a body parser.
Not handling errors on the request or response streams.
Setting headers after calling res.write or res.end.

questions.title: process: env, argv, exit codes
questions.question: What is on the process object that you use day to day? What is the difference between process.exit() and setting process.exitCode?
questions.short: `process.env` holds environment variables as strings, `process.argv` holds the command line arguments, and `process.exitCode` sets the code the process will exit with. `process.exit(code)` stops the process immediately, even if there is pending async work, so buffered logs or in-flight writes can be lost. Setting `process.exitCode` and letting the event loop drain is safer: Node exits naturally when nothing is left to do, with that code.
questions.simple: process.exit() is pulling the plug on a computer. Setting exitCode is choosing "shut down" and letting open programs save first.

head: Property / method
Use
rows: Environment variables. Values are always strings: `process.env.PORT ?? '3000'`.
High-resolution monotonic time for measuring durations.
Code used when the process exits on its own.

explain.caption: util.parseArgs is built in (stable since Node 20).

list: 0: success. 1: generic failure, also used for uncaught exceptions.
Killed by a signal: shells and Docker report 128 + signal number, so SIGTERM shows as 143 and SIGKILL as 137 (often an OOM kill).
CI, Kubernetes and process managers look at the code to decide whether a job failed.

explain.p: `process.exit()` runs `'exit'` listeners synchronously and then stops. Async work inside `'exit'` listeners never finishes. Writes to stdout that are pipes can be asynchronous on POSIX, which is why log lines sometimes vanish after `process.exit()`.

list: `'beforeExit'`: emitted when the loop becomes empty. You may schedule more async work here and the process keeps running. Not emitted on `process.exit()` or uncaught exceptions.
`'exit'`: last chance, synchronous code only.

explain.note: Since Node 15, an unhandled promise rejection crashes the process by default (`--unhandled-rejections=throw`). Do not rely on it as a log message.

anim.title: Letting the event loop drain before exit

steps.note: We register a 'beforeExit' listener. It fires when the event loop has nothing left to do.
The 'exit' listener runs at the very end. Only sync code works there.
A timer is a pending handle. While it exists, the event loop stays alive.
The main script finishes, but Node does not exit: the timer still keeps the loop alive.
After about 10 ms the timer callback runs. If we had called process.exit() in main, this would never print.
Nothing is pending now, so Node emits 'beforeExit' with code 0. A listener could schedule more work here.
Still nothing pending, so Node emits 'exit' and the process ends with code 0.

followups.q: How do you validate environment variables?
followups.a: Parse them once at startup into a typed config object (for example with Zod), fail fast with a clear message if something is missing, and never read process.env deep inside business logic.

followups.q: Is reading process.env expensive?
followups.a: Each access goes through a getter into the C++ environment, so it is slower than a normal object property. Reading it once into a config object avoids that and is cleaner.

followups.q: Should you keep running after 'uncaughtException'?
followups.a: No. The process state may be corrupted. Log it, try to flush, and exit with a non-zero code; let the process manager restart it.

mistakes: Calling process.exit() right after an async log or DB write.
Forgetting that env values are strings, so `process.env.DEBUG === true` is never true.
Doing async work in an 'exit' listener.

questions.title: Graceful shutdown
questions.question: Your Node API runs in Kubernetes. How do you handle SIGTERM so deploys do not drop requests?
questions.short: On SIGTERM I stop accepting new connections with `server.close()`, let in-flight requests finish, close idle keep-alive connections, then close resources like DB pools, queue consumers and Redis clients, and exit. I also start a hard timeout (shorter than the platform grace period, which is 30 seconds by default in Kubernetes) that force-exits if something hangs. It is also common to fail the readiness probe first so the load balancer stops sending traffic.
questions.simple: It is like closing a restaurant: lock the front door, let the guests who are eating finish, clean the kitchen, then turn off the lights. If a guest refuses to leave after 10 minutes, you call it a night anyway.

list: `SIGTERM`: polite "please stop". Sent by Kubernetes, Docker `stop`, systemd and most process managers.
`SIGINT`: Ctrl+C in a terminal.
`SIGKILL`: cannot be caught. Sent when the grace period runs out.
If you add a listener for SIGTERM or SIGINT, Node no longer exits by default; you are responsible for exiting.

`server.close()` stops new connections but waits for existing ones. Keep-alive connections can sit idle and keep the server open. Since Node 19, `close()` also closes idle connections; on older versions call `server.closeIdleConnections()`. `server.closeAllConnections()` is the hard option.

Kubernetes removes the pod from endpoints at the same time as it sends SIGTERM, not before. Many teams flip readiness to failing and wait a few seconds before closing the server so the load balancer stops routing new traffic.
If your container runs `npm start`, npm may not forward signals well. Run `node server.js` directly as the CMD, or use an init like `tini`.
Long-lived connections (WebSockets, SSE) never finish by themselves; close them explicitly.

explain.note: The hard timeout must be shorter than `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, otherwise Kubernetes sends SIGKILL first and your logs never show what hung.

anim.title: SIGTERM shutdown sequence

steps.note: Normal operation: the server accepts connections and handles requests using the DB pool.
Kubernetes sends SIGTERM. Our listener runs instead of Node exiting immediately.
We set a flag so a second signal (for example a double Ctrl+C) does not start shutdown twice.
A safety timer starts. unref() means it will not keep the process alive if everything closes in time.
server.close() stops accepting new connections at once. Existing requests are allowed to finish.
GET /a finishes and its connection closes. POST /b is still working, and it still needs the DB, which is why we do not close the pool yet.
POST /b finishes. All connections are closed, so the close callback fires and the await resolves.
Now it is safe to close the DB pool. pool.end() waits for connections to be released and closes them.
Everything is closed. The only thing left is the unref-ed timer, which does not keep the loop alive, so Node exits with code 0.

followups.q: What if a request takes longer than the timeout?
followups.a: The forced exit kills it. Set the timeout based on your slowest normal request, and make long jobs resumable or move them to a queue so a restart is safe.

followups.q: Why not just call process.exit(0) in the SIGTERM handler?
followups.a: That drops every in-flight request and may lose buffered logs and unflushed writes, which is exactly what graceful shutdown is meant to avoid.

followups.q: How do you test graceful shutdown?
followups.a: Start the app, fire a slow request, send SIGTERM with `kill -TERM <pid>`, and assert that the request completes, new connections are refused and the process exits with 0 before the timeout.

mistakes: Closing the DB pool before in-flight requests have finished.
Forgetting keep-alive and WebSocket connections, so server.close() never completes.
No hard timeout, so a stuck handler blocks the deploy until SIGKILL.
Running the app via `npm start` in Docker and never receiving SIGTERM in Node.

questions.title: The cluster module
questions.question: How does the cluster module let several Node processes listen on the same port?
questions.short: cluster.fork() starts copies of the same script as separate processes. The primary process owns the listening socket: by default on Linux and macOS it accepts connections and hands them to workers round-robin over IPC; on Windows the workers share the handle and the OS distributes. Each worker has its own memory and event loop, so you get multi-core use, but no shared in-memory state. Today many teams skip cluster and run one process per container, letting Kubernetes or PM2 do the scaling.
questions.simple: The primary is a host at a restaurant door who seats each new guest at the next waiter in turn. Each waiter works alone and does not share notes with the others.

list: When a worker calls `listen(3000)`, it asks the primary over IPC. The primary creates the real listening socket once.
`SCHED_RR` (default except on Windows): the primary accepts each connection and passes the socket handle to the next worker.
`SCHED_NONE`: workers get the listening handle and the OS decides who accepts. This can be unbalanced.

explain.h: Things that break when you cluster

list: In-memory sessions, caches and rate limiters are per worker. Move them to Redis or a database.
Scheduled jobs (cron) run once per worker unless you guard them.
WebSockets need sticky sessions if you use a fallback transport that spans requests.

explain.p: In Kubernetes you usually run one Node process per container and scale with replicas. That gives clean restarts, per-process metrics and simpler memory limits. cluster or PM2 cluster mode is more useful on a single VM.

explain.note: The primary should do almost nothing except manage workers. If it crashes, all workers go down.

anim.title: Primary hands connections to workers

steps.note: The script starts as the primary process. isPrimary is true.
fork() starts the same script again as new processes. Here the machine has 3 cores, so we get 3 workers.
In each worker isPrimary is false, so it calls listen(3000). The request goes to the primary, which opens the real socket once.
Three connections arrive. The primary accepts them.
Round-robin: A goes to W1, B to W2, C to W3. Each worker handles its connection on its own event loop.
W2 crashes. The primary gets an exit event. Other workers keep serving.
The primary forks a replacement, which registers for the same port.

followups.q: Can workers share memory?
followups.a: No. They are separate processes. They can message the primary with `process.send()` / `worker.send()`, but shared state belongs in Redis or a database.

followups.q: How do you do zero-downtime restarts with cluster?
followups.a: Restart workers one at a time: fork a new one, wait for it to be listening, then disconnect an old one so it finishes its requests and exits.

followups.q: Is cluster the same as worker_threads?
followups.a: No. cluster creates processes to scale network servers across cores. worker_threads creates threads inside one process for CPU-heavy work.

mistakes: Storing sessions or rate-limit counters in memory with cluster enabled.
Using cluster inside Kubernetes pods with a 1-CPU limit, which only adds overhead.
Thinking cluster makes one request faster. It increases throughput, not single-request speed.

questions.title: worker_threads
questions.question: When would you use worker_threads? How do threads communicate, and what are SharedArrayBuffer and transferring?
questions.short: I use worker_threads for CPU-heavy JavaScript like image processing, parsing big files, compression or hashing, so the main event loop stays responsive. Each worker has its own V8 isolate, event loop and heap. They talk with postMessage, which copies data with the structured clone algorithm; you can transfer an ArrayBuffer to move it with zero copy, or use a SharedArrayBuffer with Atomics to share the same memory. For I/O, threads do not help because Node already does I/O asynchronously.
questions.simple: A worker is a second cook in a separate kitchen. You pass ingredients through a hatch (postMessage). Transferring hands over the bowl itself, and a SharedArrayBuffer is a counter both kitchens can reach.

head: Method
Cost
After sending
rows: Both sides have their own copy
The sender loses access; its ArrayBuffer becomes empty (detached)
Both threads see the same memory; coordinate with `Atomics`

explain.p: Starting a worker costs a few milliseconds and some memory for a new V8 isolate. For a server, create a fixed pool at startup (roughly one per core) and send tasks to idle workers. Libraries like `piscina` do this well.

list: For database calls, HTTP calls or file reads: these are already async.
For tiny tasks where the copy cost is bigger than the work.
As a replacement for horizontal scaling.

explain.note: Functions, class instances with methods, and sockets cannot be cloned. Send plain data. Some handles (like `MessagePort`) can be transferred.

anim.title: Main thread stays free while the worker computes

steps.note: The worker code is a string here only to keep the demo in one file; normally it is a separate file.
new Worker starts a new thread with its own V8 isolate and event loop. workerData (100) is cloned into it.
The constructor returned right away. The main thread does not wait for the worker.
We attach listeners for the result and for the exit.
The main thread keeps running its own code while the worker computes in parallel.
The worker finishes the sum and calls postMessage. The number is cloned into the message channel.
The main event loop picks up the message and runs the 'message' listener.
The worker has nothing left to do, so its loop ends and the 'exit' event fires with code 0.

followups.q: Does a worker share the libuv thread pool?
followups.a: Yes. All threads in the process share the same libuv thread pool for fs, crypto and zlib work, so many workers doing file I/O can still saturate it.

followups.q: What happens if a worker throws?
followups.a: The worker emits 'error' in the main thread with the error, then 'exit' with a non-zero code. The main process does not crash unless the 'error' event is unhandled.

followups.q: How do you limit a worker memory?
followups.a: Pass `resourceLimits` such as `maxOldGenerationSizeMb` in the Worker options. If exceeded, the worker is terminated, not the whole process.

mistakes: Using worker_threads to speed up database or HTTP calls.
Creating a new worker for every request instead of using a pool.
Using a transferred ArrayBuffer after sending it.
Sharing memory through SharedArrayBuffer without Atomics and getting race conditions.

questions.title: child_process: spawn, exec, execFile, fork
questions.question: What is the difference between spawn, exec, execFile and fork? Why is exec dangerous with user input?
questions.short: `spawn` starts a program and gives you streaming stdout/stderr, good for long-running or large output. `exec` runs a command string through a shell and buffers all output into memory, up to maxBuffer. `execFile` runs a file directly with an argument array and no shell, also buffered. `fork` is a special spawn for Node scripts that adds an IPC channel for `send()`/`on("message")`. exec is dangerous because the string goes to a shell, so user input containing `;` or `$(...)` becomes shell injection; use execFile or spawn with an argument array instead.
questions.simple: exec is like dictating a sentence to someone who obeys every word, including any extra orders a stranger slipped in. execFile hands over a form with fixed boxes, so extra text is just text.

head: Function
Shell?
Output
Best for
rows: Running a binary with arguments safely
Inherits parent stdio by default + IPC channel
Child Node.js processes that exchange messages

explain.p: With `execFile` or `spawn` without `shell: true`, arguments go straight to the OS as an array. Shell characters have no special meaning. You should still validate inputs, because the program itself may interpret options like `--output`.

explain.note: Always handle the child's 'error' event (spawn failure) and 'close'/'exit' (non-zero code). Also pass a timeout or an AbortSignal so a stuck child does not live forever.

followups.q: What is the difference between 'exit' and 'close' on a child?
followups.a: 'exit' fires when the process ends; its stdio streams may still have data. 'close' fires after the process ended and all its stdio streams closed, so all output has been read.

followups.q: What happens if exec output exceeds maxBuffer?
followups.a: The child is killed and the callback gets an error. For large output use spawn and stream it.

followups.q: Does a child process die when the parent dies?
followups.a: No, not automatically: a child keeps running if the parent exits or crashes. Kill children on shutdown, and use `detached` and `unref()` only when you really want it to outlive the parent.

mistakes: Building exec command strings with user input.
Using exec for commands that output a lot of data, then hitting maxBuffer.
Not listening for the 'error' event, so a missing binary crashes the app.
Thinking `spawn(..., { shell: true })` is as safe as plain spawn.

questions.title: cluster vs worker_threads vs child_process
questions.question: Compare cluster, worker_threads and child_process. Which would you pick for which problem?
questions.short: cluster forks copies of your server as separate processes to use all cores for handling network requests. worker_threads runs JavaScript on extra threads in the same process for CPU-heavy work, with cheap message passing and optional shared memory. child_process runs any other program, or another Node script with fork, in a fully isolated process. So: more request throughput is cluster or more containers, heavy computation is worker_threads, external tools or strong isolation is child_process.
questions.simple: cluster is opening more identical shops. worker_threads is hiring helpers in the back of the same shop. child_process is calling an outside company to do a job.

head: cluster
worker_threads
child_process
rows: One worker dies, primary restarts it
Child dies; parent gets exit code
Scale HTTP across cores on one VM

list: The event loop is blocked by CPU work in your own JS: worker_threads (with a pool).
You need to call a non-Node tool: child_process (execFile/spawn).
You need to isolate risky or memory-leaky code completely, or run untrusted plugins: child_process (fork) or a separate service.
You want more requests per second on one big VM: cluster or PM2. In Kubernetes: more pods.

explain.note: None of these help with slow I/O like a slow database. That needs better queries, caching or concurrency control, not more threads.

followups.q: Can you combine them?
followups.a: Yes. A clustered server can have a worker_threads pool in each worker. Just budget cores: N processes each with M threads can oversubscribe the CPU.

followups.q: Why is a crash in a worker thread less severe than in the main thread?
followups.a: An uncaught error in a worker ends only that worker and is reported to the main thread as an event. An uncaught error on the main thread kills the whole process.

mistakes: Using cluster to fix a CPU-heavy endpoint. Each request is still blocking its own worker.
Using worker_threads to run shell commands.
Forgetting that all three cost memory and start-up time.

questions.title: crypto basics
questions.question: Which crypto functions do you use in a typical backend? How should you compare secrets like API keys or HMAC signatures?
questions.short: I use `crypto.randomUUID()` for ids, `randomBytes` for tokens, `createHash("sha256")` for checksums, `createHmac` for signing webhooks, and `scrypt` (or bcrypt/argon2 libraries) for passwords; never plain SHA for passwords. To compare secrets I use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers, because `===` stops at the first different character and the timing difference can leak the secret.
questions.simple: A normal comparison is like a guard who sends you away the moment the first letter of your password is wrong, so you can guess letter by letter by watching how fast he answers. timingSafeEqual always checks every letter.

explain.code:
const crypto = require('node:crypto');

crypto.randomUUID();                          // 'b3e1...' v4 UUID
crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'); // session / reset token
crypto.randomInt(100000, 1000000);            // 6-digit code, unbiased

crypto.createHash('sha256').update(fileBuffer).digest('hex');      // checksum
crypto.createHmac('sha256', secret).update(rawBody).digest('hex'); // webhook signature

explain.p: Note that the HMAC must be computed over the exact raw bytes received. If you parse JSON and stringify it again, spacing changes and the signature will not match. In Express, use `express.raw()` for that route.

list: Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256) are wrong for passwords: attackers can try billions per second.
Use a slow, salted algorithm: scrypt (built in), bcrypt or argon2 (npm packages).
Async `scrypt`/`pbkdf2` run on the libuv thread pool; the `Sync` versions block the event loop.

explain.note: `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure. Never use it for tokens, ids that must be unguessable, or OTP codes.

followups.q: Why does crypto work slow down unrelated file reads?
followups.a: Async crypto like pbkdf2 and scrypt uses the same 4-thread libuv pool as fs. Many login requests can fill the pool and delay file I/O.

followups.q: Hash vs HMAC vs encryption?
followups.a: A hash is a one-way fingerprint. An HMAC is a hash mixed with a secret key, proving the sender knew the key. Encryption (e.g. AES-256-GCM via createCipheriv) is reversible with the key.

followups.q: Is randomUUID safe as a secret token?
followups.a: It uses a secure random generator and has 122 random bits, so it is unguessable, but a dedicated `randomBytes(32)` token is clearer and has more entropy.

mistakes: Comparing signatures or tokens with ===.
Hashing passwords with SHA-256 or MD5.
Calling timingSafeEqual on buffers of different length and crashing.
Computing the webhook HMAC over re-serialized JSON instead of the raw body.

questions.title: The os module
questions.question: What do you use the os module for in a backend service?
questions.short: Mostly for sizing and diagnostics: `os.availableParallelism()` (or `os.cpus().length`) to decide how many workers to start, `os.totalmem()` and `os.freemem()` for memory info, `os.hostname()` for logs, `os.tmpdir()` for temp files and `os.EOL` for line endings. In containers, be careful: these can report the host machine, not the container limits.
questions.simple: The os module is the dashboard of the machine your app is running on: how many engines, how much fuel, what the car is called.

explain.p: Inside Docker or Kubernetes with CPU limits, `os.cpus().length` usually returns the number of CPUs on the host, which could be 64 even if your pod is limited to 2. Starting 64 workers would hurt. `os.availableParallelism()` respects CPU affinity but not necessarily cgroup CPU quotas, so for container sizing it is often best to set worker counts from an env variable.

Similarly, `os.totalmem()` may show host memory. V8 picks its default heap limit from the memory it sees, which may not match your container limit, so set `--max-old-space-size` to fit your container limit when it matters.

list: Pool sizes for worker_threads or cluster.
Adding hostname and pid to every log line.
Health or debug endpoints exposing load and memory.
Creating temp directories with `fs.mkdtemp(path.join(os.tmpdir(), "app-"))`.

followups.q: How do you see how much memory your own process uses?
followups.a: Use `process.memoryUsage()`: rss is total resident memory, heapUsed is the JS heap in use, external and arrayBuffers are memory outside the V8 heap such as Buffers.

followups.q: Is os.freemem() a good health signal?
followups.a: Not really on Linux, where free memory is often low because the kernel uses it for caches. Process RSS against your container limit is more useful.

mistakes: Sizing worker pools from os.cpus().length inside a CPU-limited container.
Using os.freemem() alone to decide that the server is out of memory.

questions.title: Timers: ref and unref
questions.question: What do timer.unref() and timer.ref() do, and where are they useful?
questions.short: By default a timer keeps the event loop alive: Node will not exit while it is pending. `unref()` tells Node "do not keep the process alive just for this timer"; it still fires if the process is running for other reasons. `ref()` undoes that. It is useful for background tasks like metrics flushes, cache cleanup intervals or shutdown watchdog timers that should never block the process from exiting.
questions.simple: A ref-ed timer is a guest who must leave before you can lock the house. An unref-ed timer is a cat: you lock up even if the cat is still inside.

explain.p: Node exits when there are no more ref-ed handles (timers, sockets, servers, child processes) and no pending requests. Every handle has a ref flag. `unref()` clears it, `ref()` sets it again, and `hasRef()` tells you the current value.

list: `server.unref()`: a server that should not keep the process alive by itself.
`socket.unref()`, `childProcess.unref()` (with `detached: true` to let a child outlive the parent).
`worker.unref()` for a worker thread.

explain.p: A test runner or script that "hangs after finishing" is often kept alive by an open handle: an interval, a DB pool or a server that was never closed. The right fix is usually to close it; `unref()` is right only for things that truly are optional background work.

explain.note: In the promise API, `timers/promises` `setTimeout(ms, value, { ref: false })` gives you an unref-ed timer you can await.

anim.title: An unref-ed timer does not keep Node alive

steps.note: A 1 second timer is created. Like every timer, it starts ref-ed, so it would keep Node running.
unref() moves it out of the set of things that keep the process alive. It can still fire if Node is alive anyway.
hasRef() confirms the flag is now false.
A normal 10 ms timer. This one is ref-ed and keeps the loop alive.
Main code finishes. Node checks: is there any ref-ed handle? Yes, the 10 ms timer, so it keeps running.
The 10 ms timer fires and is removed.
Now only the unref-ed 1 second timer remains. It does not count, so Node exits and 'never printed' never prints.

followups.q: How do you find what keeps a process alive?
followups.a: `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` lists the types of active resources (like 'Timeout' or 'TCPSocketWrap'). Test runners also have flags to detect open handles, like Jest's `--detectOpenHandles`.

followups.q: Does unref() cancel the timer?
followups.a: No. It only changes whether the timer keeps the process alive. Use clearTimeout to cancel it.

mistakes: Using unref() to hide a resource that should have been closed, like a DB pool in tests.
Thinking unref() cancels the timer.
Forgetting unref() on the shutdown watchdog, so a clean shutdown still waits the full timeout.
